title: Sea surface temperature in the Northeast Pacific
text:
Sea surface temperature (SST) and its anomalies, or deviations above or below the “normal” conditions, are important to monitor over time. Variations that happen for an extended period of time, or are large in magnitude, may have significant impacts on the wider ecosystem. Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are a topic of growing concern, as large-scale heat events can negatively affect the life cycles, food availability, and habitat of so many species that live in our oceans. MHWs are typically defined as temperatures above the upper 90th percentile of what is typical for a given area Hobday et al. (2018). On the other hand, Marine cold spells (MCSs), are periods where temperatures are cooler than the lower 10th percentile typically observed in a location, and may also have both positive and negative effects on ecosystems (see Schlegel et al. 2021 for more).





Bull kelp, Nereocystis luetkeana, a species negatively impacted by marine heatwaves. Image from Wikimedia Commons, license CC BY SA 2.0.

title: Sea surface temperature in the Northeast Pacific
section: How does SST in the Northeast Pacific compare between years?
text:
How does SST in the Northeast Pacific compare between years?
The average SST and SST anomaly of the NEP is shown below, beginning in 1981. A few years have been selected for further emphasis. 2014 and 2015, years of “the Blob”, are shown in pink and purple. 2019, another anomalously warm year occurring during an El Nino, is shown in cyan. The most recent three years, which have also been some of the warmest on record, are shown as orange (2023), brown (2024), and red (2025). 2026 progress is shown in black.


Rankings of 10 warmest years since 1981

When averaging the SST and SST anomaly for each year for the entire NEP (right), the years of “the Blob” were the warmest overall since 1981. 2025 ranked at number 5, behind 2019 and 2020.
Below are top 10 rankings of SST when averaged for the entire NEP by month. Click on the tab to alternate between the averaged SST and SST anomaly.








Mean monthly SSTMean monthly SST anomaly


The point indicates the mean of the SST by month, with the bars indicating the monthly standard deviation bounds. The years are indicated on the left, with warmest indicated with a rank of “1.”  


The point indicates the mean SST anomaly by month, with the bars indicating the monthly mean anomaly standard deviation bounds. The years are indicated on the left, with highest mean anomaly indicated with a rank of “1.”  





Annual mean anomaly SST trend
The mean annual SST anomaly of the NEP, beginning in 1982, is below. The trendline was calculated using a linear least-squares model.
The points indicate the mean SST anomaly by year, with 2026 indicated in orange.

title: About
Buoy temperature in the Canadian Pacific Exclusive Economic Zone and Northeast Pacific
text: When using sea surface temperature datasets to monitor marine heatwaves (MHWs), it is important to compare them to other data sources. Here, we assembled temperatures measured by buoys located in the Canadian Pacific EEZ, as well as further throughout the Northeast Pacific (NEP).

title: Buoy temperature in the Canadian Pacific Exclusive Economic Zone and Northeast Pacific

title: Buoy temperature in the Canadian Pacific Exclusive Economic Zone and Northeast Pacific
text:
Northeast Pacific buoy temperatures
In addition to the ECCC buoy data, NOAA’s National Buoy Data Center reports temperature data from buoys, with many time series dating back more than 30 years. Data from NDBC buoys have been added below, so that we can view current SSTs and SST anomalies throughout the Northeast Pacific ocean.

NDBC buoy data

Dataset: NDBC Standard Meteorological Buoy Data
Data access: NOAA Coastwatch West Coast Regional Node ERDDAP cwwcNDBCMet record
Climatology period: 1991–2020 (where available)







NoteClick here to view map of buoys



















NoteClick here to view 1991-2020 buoy surface temperature climatologies












The 1991-2020 temperature climatologies of each buoy are shown. The lines are coloured by latitude, with yellow indicating the buoys located further south, and purple indicating the buoys located in the northern Gulf of Alaska.







Latest week of data



Coloured circles indicate the weekly SST and SST anomaly at buoy locations (see collapsed location maps above), averaged weekly to correspond to the OISST maps on the previous page.








Note2026 NDBC buoy SST and SST anomalies





The white lines outlined in black are daily mean observations from 2026. The buoy climatological mean (grey line) is plotted with 10th and 90th percentiles (grey shading). The climatology spans 1991–2020, though some buoys began collecting data later: C46246 Ocean Station Papa and C46087 Neah Bay.
